caution: A failure to reproduce is not a finding that the paper is wrong. It may be a failure of the attempt.

attempts.label: CRCNS:ppc-1
attempts.entry_title: Limb position, vision and area 5 activity (Shi, Apker and Buneo 2013)
attempts.summary: In this area 5 dataset, which holds only one of the paper's two monkeys, the central neural result held up: as many neurons coded static hand position during the hold as reported, and fewer were modulated by vision of the hand. Decoding was better and spike timing less irregular with the hand visible, though both directions rest on a guess at which undocumented trial code means vision. Decoding accuracies, the Fano factor difference and the strength of visual suppression matched only in part or not at all. Hand endpoints differed between conditions in 16% of sessions against the paper's 6.9%, and whether the stored position is a hold mean is undocumented. Eye-position and aborted-trial controls could not be tested.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Shi, Apker and Buneo (2013) on CRCNS ppc-1, which holds the sorted spikes and trial events of area 5 recordings while monkeys held the arm at eight targets with or without vision of a cursor. It compares hand positions, ANOVA effect counts, suppression indexes, variability and decoding between the Vision and No Vision conditions. The data set holds monkey X's sessions only, and which condition code is Vision is inferred from the data.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Shi et al. (2013) from CRCNS ppc-1

outcomes.statement: Few sessions showed a significant difference in mean arm endpoint position between V and NV at a target; the average percentage across animals and targets was 6.9 +/- 1.5% (one-factor MANOVA, P < 0.05).
outcomes.quote: The average percentage of sessions (across animals and targets) with a significant difference in mean position was 6.9
outcomes.notes: In 2,872 session and target pairs of 359 monkey X sessions, 16.1% show a significant V against NV difference by the two-group MANOVA (Hotelling T squared), both as the mean of the 8 target percentages (16.12, SD 4.27 over targets) and pooled (16.12), against 6.9 +/- 1.5%. Per target the percentage runs from 9.2 to 22.8%. With the V and NV labels shuffled within each session and target the MANOVA rejects in 5.7% of pairs, and the conditions are interleaved within sessions (median 39 runs of one condition against 41 for a random order), so neither the test nor slow drift accounts for the 16%. Within a session the five trials at a target spread by a median SD of 0.29, 0.29 and 0.19 cm in x, y, z.
deviations: Monkey X only; the data set holds no monkey B session, so the average is over 8 targets of one animal, not 16 animal and target cells.

Each trial has one hand position in the data (fields 19 to 21 of the trial's text record), not a position trace, so the MANOVA uses that value in place of the trial's mean over the 800 ms hold (Fig. 2 legend). That it is the hold endpoint is read from the data (its target means match Table 1 within its SDs); the data set does not say whether it is a hold mean or one sample. No analog channel of the three sessions summarised follows the hand, so it cannot be checked against a trace.
V and NV are codes 4 and 7 of the record's field 14 under an assumed mapping; the test is symmetric in V and NV, so the mapping does not change it.

outcomes.statement: Few sessions showed a significant difference in endpoint variability between V and NV; along the horizontal, vertical and depth axes the average percentages were 5 +/- 1.9%, 4.7 +/- 1.6% and 6 +/- 0.9% (Levene's test, P < 0.05).
outcomes.quote: Similarly, the average percentages of sessions with a significant difference in variability along the horizontal, vertical, and depth axes were 5
outcomes.notes: With Levene's test centred on the mean, 8.08, 8.08 and 7.00% of pairs differ in x, y and z (mean of target percentages, the same pooled), against 5 +/- 1.9, 4.7 +/- 1.6 and 6 +/- 0.9; z is within tolerance, x and y are not. Centred on the median, 0.45, 0.66 and 0.42%. No reading puts all three axes within tolerance.
deviations: Monkey X only, and one hand position per trial, as for behavior-mean-position-sessions.

outcomes.statement: Mean endpoint positions per target in the V and NV conditions are those of Table 1, and differ between conditions by at most 0.11 cm at every target, coordinate and animal.
outcomes.inferred: Values read from Table 1, whose legend gives only the units and the sample; no sentence states them. The at most 0.11 cm difference is a reading of the table, used in the Results to say the holding behavior was largely the same.
outcomes.notes: All 48 of monkey X's means (8 targets, 3 axes, 2 conditions; mean over 359 sessions of the session means) are within the Table 1 SDs, also after removing the mean offsets (-0.10, -0.17 and +0.26 cm in x, y, z). The largest V minus NV difference of the means is 0.150 cm (135 degrees, y), above the 0.121 cm bound, so the second part of the criterion fails. Monkey B's 48 values cannot be tested. No measured list is given, as the 48 monkey B values have no counterpart.
deviations: Monkey X only; 359 sessions against the paper's 219.
One hand position per trial, as for behavior-mean-position-sessions.

outcomes.statement: The across-session SDs of endpoint position per target are those of Table 1, about 0.5 to 1.3 cm for monkey X and 0.4 to 0.6 cm for monkey B.
outcomes.inferred: Values read from Table 1; no sentence states them.
outcomes.notes: 4 of monkey X's 48 SDs over sessions (8.3%) are within 10% of Table 1. The SDs run from 0.32 to 0.67 cm against 0.50 to 1.28 cm in Table 1, a median 0.55 times the paper's. The SD over all trials pooled across sessions (a variant) runs from 0.41 to 0.73 cm, 14.6% within.
deviations: Monkey X only; 359 sessions against the paper's 219, which may differ in their spread.

outcomes.statement: An example neuron fired most when the hand was held at the lower left target (225 degrees) in both V and NV; its hold-period rate showed a main effect of position (P < 0.05) but no effect of vision (P = 0.52) and no interaction (P = 0.64).
outcomes.quote: For both the V and NV conditions, discharge was greatest when the animal held its hand at the target located in the lower left part of the workspace (225

statistics.n: one neuron, 8 targets, V and NV trials

statistics.about: main effect of the visual conditions

outcomes.notes: Of 359 units (first unit per session), 8 have their maximal mean rate at 225 degrees in both conditions and a position effect (10 of 483 among all units). None has vision and interaction P values within 0.52 +/- 0.052 and 0.64 +/- 0.064. The closest, 073009_4 chan1a, has P = 0.364 and 0.537 (measured). The paper does not identify the neuron, and it may be one of monkey B's, absent here.
deviations: Monkey X only.

outcomes.statement: In a 500 ms epoch centred on movement onset, 41% (139 of 343) of neurons were modulated by the movement vector (main and/or interaction effects, ANOVA, P < 0.05).
outcomes.quote: when data during a 500-ms epoch centered on movement onset were analyzed, 41% (139/ 343) of the neurons were found to be modulated by the required movement vector
outcomes.notes: With movement onset at event code 8, 187 of 359 units (52.1%, 179 scaled to 343) have a target main effect or interaction in the 500 ms centred on it, against 139 +/- 13.9 (41%). All 483 units give 49.9% (171 scaled). A window centred on the target-code event (the cursor entering the target window) gives 65.5%, and one on code 3 (target onset) 6.1%. Question for the paper's authors, how movement onset was defined (methods_unavailable finding).
deviations: Movement onset is taken as event code 8 (reading (a) of the criterion, an event code). The data set does not document the codes; code 8 comes 0.22 to 0.58 s after code 3 (read as target onset) and 0.03 to 0.38 s before the target code event (5th to 95th percentiles; the full ranges are 0.08 to 1.12 s and 0.02 to 1.25 s), which fits the cursor leaving the start window, the definition of reading (b). No continuous arm position is in the data set to run reading (b) directly. This reading of the code is an assumption.
Monkey X only, 359 units; counts compared as percentages, scaled to 343.

outcomes.statement: In the 800 ms static holding period, 39% (135 of 343) of neurons showed a significant main effect of position.
outcomes.quote: When data from the 800-ms static holding period were considered, 39% (135/343) of the neurons showed a significant main effect of position
outcomes.notes: 141 of 359 units (39.3%, 135 scaled to 343) have a position main effect in the two-factor ANOVA of the last 800 ms of the hold, against 135 of 343 (39.4%). The smoothed PSTH rate (sigma 50 ms) gives 142 (39.6%) and all 483 sorted units 176 (36.4%, 125 scaled), both within tolerance. Shuffled labels give 4.2% significant.
deviations: Monkey X only; 359 sessions with the complete design (5 completed trials per target and condition; the first five where a session has more), one unit per session (the first sorted unit), against 343 neurons from two monkeys. The count is compared as a percentage, scaled to 343.

The end of the hold is event code 12, read from the data: it follows code 10 (read as target offset) by 0.83 to 1.86 s, and on every completed trial by at least the record's minimum hold (field 11) plus 28 ms; the window is the 800 ms before it. In 11.6% of trials the window starts less than 250 ms after code 10.

outcomes.statement: Only 13% (44 of 343) of neurons showed a main effect of the visual conditions in the holding period.
outcomes.quote: while only 13% (44/343) showed a main effect of the visual conditions
outcomes.notes: 49 of 359 units (13.6%, 47 scaled to 343) have a vision main effect, against 44 +/- 4.4, and fewer than the 141 with a position effect. All units give 69 of 483 (14.3%, 49 scaled); the PSTH rate 50 (13.9%). The count is symmetric in V and NV, so the code mapping does not change it. With all units the scaled count (49) is just above the bound of 48.4.
deviations: As for hold-position-main-effect.

One unit per session, as the paper has one neuron per session (Table 1 legend, means over 219 sessions for monkey X; Results, Behavior, N = 343 sessions for 343 neurons). Which unit of a session the paper used is not stated; the first sorted unit (a) is assumed, a standard choice. With all 483 sorted units (a variant) the outcome would differ, so it rests on this assumption. Question for the paper's authors (methods_unavailable finding).

outcomes.statement: Interaction effects of position and vision were found in 9% (27 of 343) of neurons.
outcomes.quote: Interaction effects of position and vision were found in 9% (27/343) of the neurons
outcomes.notes: 27 of 359 units (7.5%, 26 scaled to 343) have a position by vision interaction, within reading (a), 27 +/- 2.7, and outside reading (b), 31 +/- 3.1. All units give 35 of 483 (7.2%, 25 scaled).
deviations: As for hold-position-main-effect.

outcomes.statement: Similar percentages were found when the first 400 ms and the last 400 ms of the hold were analyzed separately, 31%, 9% and 5% and 29%, 10% and 4% for position main effect, vision main effect and interaction.
outcomes.quote: Similar percentages were noted when the first 400 ms and the last 400 ms of the holding period were separately analyzed (31/9/5% and 29/10/4%, respectively)
outcomes.notes: In the first and last 400 ms of the window, 35.7, 11.4 and 7.0% and 28.7, 13.6 and 5.0% of the 359 units have position, vision and interaction effects, against 31, 9, 5% and 29, 10, 4%; 1 of 6 values is within tolerance (the last 400 ms position effect). All 483 units give 31.5, 11.2, 6.2% and 27.1, 13.3, 4.3%, 3 of 6 within, which would be partial. The last 400 ms position percentage is within tolerance and the first 400 ms one is above it; the vision and interaction percentages are higher. Starting the window at least 250 ms after code 10 (a variant, against a possible saccade at its start) gives 35.7, 10.9, 7.5% and 28.8, 13.7, 5.0% (1 of 6 within), and 3 of 6 with all units.
deviations: As for hold-position-main-effect.

One unit per session, as the paper has one neuron per session (Table 1 legend, means over 219 sessions for monkey X; Results, Behavior, N = 343 sessions for 343 neurons). Which unit of a session the paper used is not stated; the first sorted unit (a) is assumed, a standard choice. With all 483 sorted units (a variant) the outcome would differ, so it rests on this assumption. Question for the paper's authors (methods_unavailable finding).

outcomes.statement: Over the full hold, 44% of neurons showed some effect of position (main and/or interaction), 19% some effect of vision, and 11% effects of both position and vision.
outcomes.quote: Overall, during the full holding period, 44% of the neurons showed some effect of position (cells with main and/or interaction effects) while 19% showed either main or interaction effects of the visual conditions. ... 11% of the neurons demonstrated effects of both position and vision (main effects of both factors and/or interaction effects)
outcomes.notes: 40.4% of units show a position effect (main or interaction), within 44 +/- 4.4; 18.7% a vision effect, within 19 +/- 1.9; 13.1% effects of both, above 11 +/- 1.1. All units give 38.3, 18.8 and 12.2%.
deviations: As for hold-position-main-effect.

outcomes.statement: Correlations between V and NV responses were the same where mean endpoint positions differed between conditions (r = 0.9301) and where they did not (r = 0.9281), so firing rate differences did not reflect endpoint differences.
outcomes.quote: We found that the correlations were identical for these two data sets (r for data set 1 ... 0.9301; r for data set 2 ... 0.9281; permutation test
outcomes.notes: With each cell's V and NV mean hold rates at a target as one pair (reading (a)), Spearman r is 0.9237 for the 463 cell and target pairs whose session and target had a significant MANOVA (data set 1) and 0.9154 for the 2,409 others (data set 2), both within 0.093 of 0.9301 and 0.9281; the permutation test finds no difference (difference 0.0083, P = 0.469). With single trials paired by order (reading (b)), r is 0.794 and 0.767, outside tolerance, and the difference of 0.027 is significant (P = 0.025). All 483 units give P = 0.267 (a) and 0.001 (b). Data set 1 is larger here than the paper's would be, as 16% of pairs had a significant MANOVA (behavior-mean-position-sessions).
deviations: The readings give different outcomes. Reading (a) is adopted as an assumption, as its r values are of the size the paper reports (0.93) and the paper speaks of correlations between the responses in the two conditions; reading (b) gives r near 0.78. Question for the paper's authors (methods_unavailable finding).
Monkey X only; one hand position per trial for the MANOVA that forms the data sets.

outcomes.statement: For most cells INDX1 was negative (activity lower with vision than without), with 84%, 77%, 85% and 84% negative among all cells, Position Only, Position/Vision and Vision Only cells (338, 110, 38 and 27 cells after outlier removal).
outcomes.quote: The percentage of cells with negative indexes was fairly consistent across the different populations (84%, 77%, 85%, and 84% for the populations shown in Fig. 4, A-D, respectively)
outcomes.notes: After outlier removal by reading (a) (Tukey fences over all cells, 3 removed), INDX1 is negative in 77.8% of all cells, 68.4% of Position Only, 75.0% of Position/Vision and 75.0% of Vision Only cells, against 84, 77, 85 and 84%; only the first is within tolerance, and the others are 0.6 to 1.5 points below their lower bounds. Readings (b) and (c) give 78.4, 70.0, 75.0, 75.0 and the same as (a). Group sizes are 356, 98, 44 and 20 (paper 338, 110, 38, 27). Among all 483 sorted units the four percentages (81.4, 71.4, 76.8, 81.2) are within tolerance. Under the other code mapping INDX1 is also mostly negative (80.5, 72.3, 74.4, 73.7%), as choosing the NV peak biases the NV rate upward.
deviations: Monkey X only, one unit per session; the population of all units, a variant, reproduces it.

One unit per session, as the paper has one neuron per session (Table 1 legend, means over 219 sessions for monkey X; Results, Behavior, N = 343 sessions for 343 neurons). Which unit of a session the paper used is not stated; the first sorted unit (a) is assumed, a standard choice. With all 483 sorted units (a variant) the outcome would differ, so it rests on this assumption. Question for the paper's authors (methods_unavailable finding).

outcomes.statement: Mean INDX1 was least negative for Position Only cells (-13%) and most negative for Position/Vision cells (-31%).
outcomes.quote: the mean INDX1 was least negative ... In contrast, the average index was most negative in the population of cells showing both positional and visual modulation by the ANOVA
outcomes.notes: Mean INDX1 is -12.0% for Position Only cells, within -13 +/- 1.3, and -24.2% for Position/Vision cells, outside -31 +/- 3.1. Position Only is the least negative of the four populations, as in the paper, but the most negative is all cells (-24.9%), not Position/Vision. Readings (b) and (c), all units (-13.7 and -26.2%) and the other code mapping (-14.2 and -27.1%) give the same pattern.
deviations: As for fig4-indx1-negative.

outcomes.statement: Among Position/Vision cells, those with their maximal response at the same or an adjacent location in the two conditions (22 of 38, 58%) had a mean INDX1 of -24%, and the others a more negative mean of -40%.
outcomes.quote: Position/Vision cells that had their maximum responses at the same or immediately adjacent locations in the two conditions (22/38; 58%) had an average index of
outcomes.notes: Of 44 Position/Vision cells, 33 (ring adjacency) or 34 (grid adjacency) have their V and NV peaks at the same or adjacent targets, against 22 of 38; their mean INDX1 is -23.0% (-23.4%), within -24 +/- 2.4, and the others' -27.6% (-26.9%), outside -40 +/- 4. All outlier readings give the same; all units give 43 or 46 of 56, -26.6 and -24.8%.
deviations: Monkey X only, one unit per session.

outcomes.statement: With an index based on each condition's own preferred location (INDX2), rate differences were weaker but still biased toward suppression, with means of -9%, -13% and -13% for Position Only, Vision Only and Position/Vision cells.
outcomes.quote: rate differences between conditions were not strong but were still biased toward suppression, with average indexes of
outcomes.notes: With outliers on INDX1 (reading (i), Tukey fences over all cells), mean INDX2 is -0.5, +12.7 and +7.5% for Position Only, Vision Only and Position/Vision cells, against -9, -13 and -13%. No outlier reading, population or code mapping gives three negative means within tolerance; the closest are outliers on INDX2 with reading (c), which gives -1.7, -10.5 and -9.5% for the 359 units and -2.0, -14.1 and -9.9% for all 483 units, where only Vision Only is within tolerance.
deviations: Monkey X only, one unit per session.

outcomes.statement: Spike rate variance at the NV preferred location tended to be higher in NV than in V, on average 56 against 30 (spikes/s)^2 across cells.
outcomes.quote: the average variance (across cells) at the peak location in the NV condition was 56 (spikes/s)2, while in the V condition the average variance was 30 (spikes/s)2
outcomes.notes: At the NV preferred location, the mean across 359 cells of the hold rate variance is 46.4 (spikes/s)^2 in NV and 23.1 in V (sample variance), higher in NV in 67% of cells, as the paper's 56 against 30, but both below tolerance. After the Fig. 4 outliers, 46.7 and 23.0; with the population variance, 37.1 and 18.5; all units, 48.5 and 25.6.
deviations: Which code is NV is assumed (code 7, from the aborts; see the attempt's findings). Under the other mapping the direction reverses.
Monkey X only, one unit per session.

outcomes.statement: The Fano factor was significantly larger in NV (1.54) than in V (1.13) (permutation test, P < 0.05).
outcomes.quote: Statistical analysis revealed that the FF was significantly larger in the NV condition (permutation test

statistics.n: spike count means and variances of all cells after outlier removal, at the NV peak location

outcomes.notes: With the Fig. 4 outliers removed (reading (a), 356 cells), FF is 1.84 in V and 3.19 in NV, larger in NV but not significantly (permutation P = 0.280 two-sided, 0.137 one-sided), and both above tolerance; a few high-rate cells (count variance up to 2,188) dominate the slope. With Tukey outliers of the count means or variances removed (reading (b), 295 cells), FF is 0.98 and 1.24, larger in NV with P = 0.020, but both below tolerance. Without removal, 1.84 and 3.18 (P = 0.280). Keeping the 331 cells whose count means and variances lie within the plotted range of Fig. 5 (0 to 80; a variant) gives 1.03 and 1.21 (P = 0.172), V within tolerance and NV not. Whether the criterion's outlier readings match the cells of Fig. 5 is asked of a reader (questions/shi-2013.yaml); the claim is tested as the file has it.
deviations: The readings give different outcomes in significance, and neither puts both FF values within tolerance. Reading (a) is adopted as an assumption, as the paper describes outlier removal only in the Fig. 4 legend. Question for the paper's authors (methods_unavailable finding).
Which code is NV is assumed, as for rate-variance-nv-higher.
Monkey X only, one unit per session.

outcomes.statement: The squared coefficient of variation of interspike intervals (CV2) was also significantly larger in NV than in V (Kruskal-Wallis test, P < 0.05).
outcomes.quote: Interestingly, the CV2, which assesses variability in the interspike intervals, was also significantly larger in the NV condition

statistics.n: CV2 of each cell in V and in NV

outcomes.notes: With the ISIs of a cell's five trials at the NV preferred location pooled (reading (a)), CV2 is larger in NV, median 0.737 against 0.622 (Kruskal-Wallis H = 5.09, P = 0.024, 318 cells, 41 without two ISIs left out). Averaged over trials (reading (b)), 0.510 against 0.456, P = 0.098, not significant. All units give P = 0.0084 (a) and 0.067 (b).
deviations: The readings give different outcomes. Reading (a) is adopted as an assumption, as the Methods say the CV2 "was calculated for each cell and condition", one value from that cell's data. Question for the paper's authors (methods_unavailable finding).
Which code is NV is assumed, as for rate-variance-nv-higher.

outcomes.statement: A maximum-likelihood decoder trained and tested on V data decoded hand position with an average accuracy across targets of 91.6 +/- 9%.
outcomes.source: Results, Neurophysiology, paragraph 7; Figure 6, top left
outcomes.quote: For example, when data from the full 800 ms of the holding period were used, average decoding accuracy across targets in the V conditions was 91.6
outcomes.notes: Trained and tested on V by the leave-one-out Poisson decoder, accuracy over 200 bootstrap resamples of the 359 cells is 77.4 +/- 6.5% (reading (a)); populations of 200 cells give 73.3% (reading (b)); both below 91.6 +/- 9%. The full population without resampling gives 87.5%. All 483 units give 68.4%. With target labels shuffled within each cell and condition, the decoder gives 16.1% (V) and 11.2% (NV) on average over 20 shuffles, near the nominal chance of 12.5%.
deviations: Which code is V is assumed; under the other mapping V/V accuracy is 63.7%, also not within, and all units give 68.4%, so the outcome does not rest on the mapping or the choice of unit.
Monkey X only, 359 cells, one per session, their trials joined by order within target and condition (criterion reading (i)).

outcomes.statement: Trained and tested on NV data, the decoder's accuracy fell to 81.9 +/- 18.0%.
outcomes.source: Results, Neurophysiology, paragraph 7; Figure 6, bottom right
outcomes.quote: In contrast, when the decoder was both trained and tested with data from the NV conditions (Fig. 6, bottom right) decoding accuracy fell to 81.9
outcomes.notes: Trained and tested on NV, accuracy is 63.7 +/- 7.0% (reading (a)), 0.2 points below the lower bound of 81.9 +/- 18.0%, and 57.2% with populations of 200 cells. The full population gives 77.5%.
deviations: Which code is NV is assumed; under the other mapping NV/NV accuracy would be 77.4%, within tolerance, so the outcome rests on the mapping.
Monkey X only, as for fig6-decoding-vv.

outcomes.statement: Decoding accuracy was significantly higher in V than in NV (t-test, P < 0.05), a small but significant role of vision in representing limb position.
outcomes.quote: The difference in decoding performance between the V and NV conditions was statistically significant
outcomes.notes: V accuracy exceeds NV accuracy, 77.4 against 63.7%, and every t-test reading finds it (paired over the 8 targets P = 0.0087; two-sample over the 200 bootstrap accuracies P = 4e-63; two-sample over targets P = 0.0081); populations of 200 cells give P = 0.0009, 6e-65 and 0.0008. With all 483 units, 68.4 against 63.0%, paired P = 0.29 and over bootstraps P = 4e-15. With all units the unpaired test over targets gives P = 0.40. With all units and populations of 200 cells, 62.9 against 55.3%, the paired test over targets also finds the difference (P = 0.036; unpaired P = 0.14). The test over bootstraps (reading (b)) treats the 200 resamples as independent, so its P value depends on how many are drawn; the tests over targets do not.
deviations: Which code is V is assumed; under the other mapping NV would decode better (77.4 against 63.7%). The mapping was chosen from aborted trials, not from neural data.

outcomes.statement: Training and testing on different conditions gave lower accuracies, 60.7 +/- 22% trained on NV and tested on V and 69.1 +/- 17% trained on V and tested on NV, so decoding degraded whenever NV data were used.
outcomes.source: Figure 6 legend; Results, Neurophysiology, paragraphs 7 and 8
outcomes.quote: Results from the analyses where the decoder ... was trained and tested with data from different conditions reinforce the idea that decoding of limb position degraded somewhat whenever data from the NV condition were used
outcomes.notes: With the leave-one-out scheme (reading (a)), trained on NV and tested on V the accuracy is 58.9% (60.7 +/- 22), trained on V and tested on NV 52.7% (69.1 +/- 17), both within tolerance and below the V/V accuracy of 77.4%. Training on all five trials (reading (b)) gives 62.1 and 56.8%. Swapping the code mapping keeps both within tolerance and below the V/V accuracy (63.7%).
deviations: Monkey X only, as for fig6-decoding-vv.

outcomes.statement: Decoding was less accurate with shorter windows, but did not differ between the first and the last 400 ms of the hold, in V or in NV.
outcomes.source: Results, Neurophysiology, paragraph 7; Discussion, Additional factors, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: While accuracy decreased with shorter windows, no difference in decoding performance was found when the first 400 ms and the last 400 ms of the holding period were compared
outcomes.notes: The 400 ms windows decode less well than the 800 ms window (V 61.2 and 66.0 against 78.3%; NV 59.8 and 42.8 against 64.6%). In V the first and last 400 ms do not differ (paired over targets P = 0.38, two-sample over targets P = 0.31; over bootstraps P = 7e-11). In NV the last 400 ms decode 17.0 points worse than the first, and every reading finds it (P = 0.0073, 0.017 and 4e-78), so the claim of no difference does not hold. The claim covers both conditions, so the code mapping does not change the outcome. With the window starting at least 250 ms after code 10 (a variant), NV still differs (57.7 against 42.8%, paired P = 0.019, unpaired over targets P = 0.031). With all 483 units the NV difference (14.6 points) is not significant over targets (paired P = 0.072, unpaired P = 0.074) and only the test over bootstraps finds it.
deviations: Monkey X only, as for fig6-decoding-vv.

One unit per session, as the paper has one neuron per session (Table 1 legend, means over 219 sessions for monkey X; Results, Behavior, N = 343 sessions for 343 neurons). Which unit of a session the paper used is not stated; the first sorted unit (a) is assumed, a standard choice. With all 483 sorted units (a variant) the outcome would differ, so it rests on this assumption. Question for the paper's authors (methods_unavailable finding).

outcomes.statement: Neurons with no ANOVA effect of position, vision or interaction still decoded position above chance at some targets, and slightly better in V than in NV (20% against 14%), though this difference was not significant.
outcomes.quote: Interestingly, average decoding accuracy was also slightly higher in the V condition than in the NV condition in this subset of cells (20% vs. 14%), similar in trend to what was observed for the entire population, though this difference was not statistically significant
outcomes.notes: The 194 of 359 cells without any ANOVA effect decode 24.7% in V and 12.5% in NV (paper 20 and 14%; neither within tolerance), V above NV and 4 targets above chance in both, but the difference is significant (paired over targets P = 0.00016), where the paper found it was not. All 483 units (266 cells without effects) give 18.3 and 17.6% (P = 0.85).
deviations: Monkey X only, as for fig6-decoding-vv.

outcomes.statement: Neither mean eye position nor the variance of its horizontal or vertical component differed between V and NV for any target (MANOVA and Levene's test).
outcomes.source: Discussion, Additional factors influencing neural responses, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: We found that neither the average eye positions nor the variances of the horizontal or vertical components of eye position differed between the V and NV conditions for any target
outcomes.notes: The data set holds no documented eye position. The analog channels are named only AD01 to AD16, and the layout of the .plxAnaAD.dat files is undocumented. Read as 7 channels of 12-bit samples at 1 kHz at the end of each file, no channel of three sessions differs between targets in the hold (one-way ANOVA P 0.15 to 1.00) or correlates with the record's hand position beyond |r| = 0.25; most saturate at +/-2047, and one spans the 16-bit range, so the layout reading is at least partly wrong. The 24 field record (224 of the 359 sessions) ends with two numbers near (0, -1.8) that might be an eye position averaged over the hold, but nothing names them; their SD within a session (0.05 to 0.07) is below the tracker's 0.25 degree resolution, which a mean of about 100 samples could reach, so the spread does not settle what they are. Tested on them for the record only (trials pooled over sessions), no target shows a V against NV difference by MANOVA, and one shows one by Levene's test (90 degrees, second value, P = 0.012 centred on the mean, 0.28 on the median); 8.7% of session and target pairs differ by MANOVA. If these fields were the mean eye position, reading (a) would therefore not reproduce the claim. The block also rests on a reading of the analog file layout known to be at least partly wrong.

outcomes.statement: In one animal, as the behavioral window around the reach targets was made smaller, aborted trials increased in both conditions, and were significantly more frequent on NV trials for smaller windows (t-test, P < 0.05), so the animals used vision to hold position.
outcomes.source: Discussion, Additional factors influencing neural responses, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: We found that as the window size decreased the number of aborted trials increased for both the NV and V conditions and, moreover, the number of these aborted trials was significantly greater on NV trials for smaller window sizes
outcomes.notes: Which condition code is NV is not documented and was inferred from the aborted trials themselves (more aborts after code 10 on code 7 trials), so a comparison of NV with V aborts would test that inference, not the paper. The window sizes are not documented either; field 1 of the record (8, 10 or 12) may be one. For the record, with field 1 at 8, 10 and 12, 31.4, 26.6 and 5.7% of code 7 trials and 13.9, 24.4 and 3.6% of code 4 trials that reached code 10 were aborted. The part that does not depend on the mapping, more aborts as the window shrinks, holds for code 7 but not for code 4 (24.4% at 10 against 13.9% at 8), if field 1 is the window size.

outcomes.statement: In a subset of sessions with the minimum hold extended to 1,200 ms, neither behavior nor neural responses differed appreciably.
outcomes.source: Discussion, Additional factors influencing neural responses, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: In a subset of experimental sessions we extended the minimum duration of the holding period out to 1,200 ms and found no appreciable differences in either the behavior of the animals or the neural responses
outcomes.notes: On every completed trial the time from code 10 to code 12 is at least the trial's own record field 11 plus 28 ms (30,789 trials; the shortest intervals, 0.83 s, are on trials with field 11 = 800, and 0.93 and 1.06 s with 900 and 1,000), so field 11 is read as the minimum hold. No completed trial in the data set has a minimum hold of 1,200 ms or more (4 aborted trials do), so the sessions with the extended hold are not in it.

findings.statement: The data descriptor gives 343 cells, 219 from monkey X and 124 from monkey B. Every session with a trial record has monkey X's target layout (targets about 9.2 cm apart horizontally and 7.4 cm vertically, middle row at y near -4 cm, depth near 10 cm, as in Table 1 for monkey X), in every month from October 2008 to November 2009; none has monkey B's square layout at a depth near 14.5 cm. Monkey B's data appear not to be in the data set.

The data set holds 359 monkey X sessions with the paper's complete design (5 completed trials per target and condition) and 485 sorted units in them (83 sessions have 2 units, 21 have 3 or 4), against the paper's 219 monkey X sessions and neurons, plus 47 sessions with an incomplete design. All were recorded on 92 days before the paper was submitted, and consecutive sessions of a day do not look like one neuron recorded again (median tuning correlation 0.04, against -0.01 across days). Which sessions and units the paper analysed is not documented.

The condition of a trial (Vision or No Vision) is coded only as 4 or 7 in field 14 of an undocumented ASCII record strobed after each trial. Nothing says which is Vision. Code 7 trials are aborted more often after the end of the reach (5,688 against 4,423) and not before it (6,040 against 6,006), which suggests 7 is No Vision; this attempt assumes so. Question for the data owners, which code is Vision.

The event codes are not described. EventCodes.txt is a generic list (TAPE = 1, DISPLAY = 10 and so on) that does not match the codes in the files (0, 1, 55, 3 to 8, the target codes 44 to 66, 10, 12, 13, 14, 255). Their meaning, and that of the 19, 22 or 24 fields of the per-trial text record (task parameters, target, condition, hand position, two further values), had to be read from their timing and values.

The analog channels (in .plx and .plxAnaAD files) are named AD01 to AD16 without description, the descriptor does not say what they record, and it lists the variables of the .plxAnaAD.mat files but not the layout of the .plxAnaAD.dat files that hold the samples. No continuous arm or eye position could be identified; the trial record gives one hand position per trial.
The descriptor gives no units for the time stamps. In the .mat files spike times are in milliseconds and event times in seconds; they agree with the .plx file of the session checked (010609_1).

Nine early files (d1 to d14.mat, 2008) have a 19 field record without hand positions and a minimum hold (record field 11) of 500 or 600 ms where the other sessions have 800 to 1,100 ms, below the paper's 800 ms hold.

Questions for the paper's authors. (1) How movement onset was defined for the 500 ms movement epoch; this attempt used event code 8, which fits the cursor leaving the start window. (2) What a response pair is in the Spearman correlations between V and NV (each cell's mean rate at a target, adopted here, or single trials). (3) Which cells were outliers in Fig. 5 (the Fig. 4 outliers were adopted here). (4) Whether CV2 pools the ISIs of a cell's trials (adopted here) or averages per trial values. (5) Which sessions and units form the 219 monkey X neurons, and which unit of a session was the session's neuron (the first sorted unit was assumed here). (6) Whether the hand position of Table 1 and the MANOVA is a mean over the hold or one sample, and whether it is the one in the record's fields 19 to 21.

entries.name: shi-2013
entries.title: Limb position, vision and area 5 activity (Shi, Apker and Buneo 2013)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Shi, Apker and Buneo (2013) on CRCNS ppc-1, which holds the sorted spikes and trial events of area 5 recordings while monkeys held the arm at eight targets with or without vision of a cursor. It compares hand positions, ANOVA effect counts, suppression indexes, variability and decoding between the Vision and No Vision conditions. The data set holds monkey X's sessions only, and which condition code is Vision is inferred from the data.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Shi et al. (2013) from CRCNS ppc-1
